title: The cost of classically simulating quantum communication is as high as it could be
authors: Riccardo Castellano, Pavel Sekatski, Nicolas Brunner
abstract: A long-standing open question is to characterize the classical communication cost of simulating the correlations arising from measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems. We consider this question in the prepare-and-measure scenario. First we construct a classical simulation model involving a finite average number of bits of one-way communication that simulates exactly the correlations arising from arbitrary $d$-dimensional quantum states and arbitrary measurements. Second, we show that no classical simulation protocol involving a finite average message dimension can exist for $d\geq 4$, hence strengthening a recent result of de Gois, Santos and Vieira. Our first result relies on a more general simulation theorem which can be applied to certain continuous variable (i.e. infinite-dimensional) quantum systems, and even beyond quantum theory, e.g. to generalized probabilistic theories. In particular, we show that multimode Gaussian states of bounded average energy and general Gaussian measurements admit an exact classical simulation with a finite expected number of bits. Overall, our results show that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is essentially as high as it could be.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the classical communication cost needed to simulate quantum correlations from measurements on qudits. It establishes a strong lower bound, showing that for dimensions $d \ge 4$, the required classical communication scales unboundedly. Overall, the results demonstrate that the classical simulation cost of quantum communication is fundamentally high, confirming the quantum advantage in this setting.
main_problem: The paper aims to characterize the fundamental classical communication cost required to simulate the correlations generated by measurements on finite-dimensional quantum systems.
main_result: It proves that for qudits of dimension $d \ge 4$, the classical simulation cost is prohibitively high (infinite expected message dimension), while simultaneously showing that for many physical systems, the cost remains finite.
method: The authors employ information-theoretic techniques, constructing classical simulation models and utilizing advanced concepts like the mass-deficit Minkowski dimension to establish lower bounds on communication complexity.
model_or_system: The primary model is the prepare-and-measure quantum communication scenario involving qudits (finite-dimensional quantum systems). The analysis is generalized to continuous variable (Gaussian) systems.
key_observables: Classical communication cost metrics include worst-case alphabet size ($\max[l_\lambda]$), expected alphabet size ($E[l_\lambda]$), and expected number of bits ($E[\log l_\lambda]$).
important_parameters: The dimension of the quantum system ($d$), the average energy bound ($E$) for Gaussian states, and the mass deficit ($\kappa_F(R)$) are key parameters.
main_assumptions: The general simulation theorem relies on the pair $(X, F)$ having a finite mass-deficit Minkowski dimension, and the Gaussian analysis assumes bounded average energy.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general simulation framework, proving a no-go result for $d \ge 4$ using expected alphabet size. It then constructs a positive simulation protocol for finite dimensions and extends the theory to continuous variable Gaussian states by bounding the mass deficit.
why_interesting: This work sets fundamental limits on what quantum correlations can be efficiently simulated classically, which is crucial for understanding the computational advantage of quantum communication protocols.
